source_text: Haec cum dicta essent, concessum est non ideo putandum aliquid iuste ac bene fieri, quia id deus, cum haec prohibenda curet, fieri tamen sinit, fatendumque esse etiam illa mala, quae contra religionem, qua deus colitur, fiunt, et dis-. plicere deo iusto et ratione iudicii eius ab omnipotente permitti; sed aliud iam esse tractandum, unde sint diuinationes uel daemonum uel quilibet illi sint, quos deos pagani uocant; uidendum enim esse, ne forte non quidem propterea haec bona putanda sint, quia ea fieri permittit omnipotens, sed ideo, quia tam magna sunt, ut nonnisi dei potentiae, tribuenda esse uideantur. ad hoc me postea responsurum esse promisi, quoniam tunc hora prodeundi ad populum iam nos urguebat, nec distuli, cum spatium datum est scribendo, et illa retexere et ista subtexere.
thought_title: God's permission does not make evil good; the question turns to the source of demonic divination
orientation: Augustine has just won the concession that God permits evil without approving it, and now he records the agreed next step: to ask where the divinations of demons or pagan gods come from.
pass_a_gloss: When these things had been said, it was conceded that something should not for that reason be thought to be done justly and well, because God, although he takes care that these things be forbidden, nevertheless allows them to be done, and that it must be admitted that even those evils, which are done against the religion by which God is worshiped, both displease the righteous God and are permitted by the Almighty by the reason of his judgment; but that another thing must now be treated, namely whence come the divinations either of demons or of whatever beings they are, whom pagans call gods; for it must be seen whether perhaps these things should not indeed for that reason be thought good, because the Almighty permits them to be done, but for this reason, because they are so great that they seem to be attributable only to the power of God. I promised that I would respond to this later, because at that time the hour for going out to the people was already pressing upon us, and I did not delay, when space was given by writing, both to unroll those things and to weave in these things.

choices.english: by the reason of his judgment
choices.why: Keeps the causal force of the ablative and the possessive eius, preserving Augustine's point that God's permission is governed by his judgment, not by approval.
Renders the indefinite concessive force of quilibet with the subjunctive, showing Augustine's refusal to grant that the pagan gods are what they claim to be.

choices.term: nonnisi dei potentiae tribuenda esse uideantur
choices.english: they seem to be attributable only to the power of God
choices.why: Preserves the restrictive nonnisi and the passive infinitive construction, keeping the appearance-verb uideantur distinct from a factual claim.
rejected: they must be ascribed to no one but God's power
they seem to belong only to divine power

choices.english: both to unroll those things and to weave in these things
choices.why: Keeps the textile metaphor of retexere and subtexere, which Augustine uses to describe his written composition as unweaving the earlier discussion and weaving in the new one.
rejected: to review those things and add these things
to unravel the former and append the latter

choices.english: the hour for going out to the people
choices.why: Renders the gerundive phrase literally, preserving the concrete pastoral context of Augustine's public duties.
rejected: the time to address the congregation
the hour of going out to preach

pass_b_english: When these things had been said, it was conceded that something is not for that reason to be thought just and good because God, while he takes care to forbid it, nevertheless allows it to happen. It must also be admitted that even those evils which are committed against the religion by which God is worshiped both displease the righteous God and are permitted by the Almighty by the reason of his judgment. But another question now had to be treated: where divinations come from—whether from demons or from whatever beings they are whom the pagans call gods. For it had to be seen whether these things should not be thought good because the Almighty permits them to happen, but rather because they are so great that they seem to be attributable only to the power of God. I promised that I would respond to this later, since the hour for going out to the people was already pressing on us. And I did not delay when time was given for writing, both to unravel those earlier arguments and to append these new ones.

problems.quote: both to unroll those things and to weave in these things
problems.source_quote: et illa retexere et ista subtexere
problems.why: retexere means 'unravel/undo,' not 'unroll'; subtexere means 'append/weave underneath,' not 'weave in.' The pair means to take apart prior arguments and add new ones.
problems.fix: both to unravel those earlier arguments and to append these new ones
problems.ruling: retexere means 'unravel/undo' not 'unroll'; subtexere means 'append/weave underneath' not 'weave in'—meaning reversed.

edits.new: both to unravel those earlier arguments and to append these new ones

fixed: Changed 'unroll' to 'unravel' and 'weave in' to 'append' to match retexere ('unravel/undo') and subtexere ('append/weave underneath'), and clarified 'those things'/'these things' as 'earlier arguments'/'new ones'.

last_rejected.quote: both to unravel those earlier arguments and to append these new ones
last_rejected.source_quote: et illa retexere et ista subtexere
last_rejected.why: "retexere" means to unweave/undo, not "unravel" in sense of clarify; "subtexere" means to weave underneath/attach, not "append". Augustine is undoing previous work and weaving in new material, not clarifying old arguments and adding new ones.
last_rejected.fix: both to unweave those earlier threads and to weave in these new ones
last_rejected.ruling: Unravel/append are valid for retexere/subtexere; meaning preserved, no reader misled.

last_rejected.quote: where divinations come from—whether from demons or from whatever beings they are whom the pagans call gods
last_rejected.source_quote: unde sint diuinationes uel daemonum uel quilibet illi sint, quos deos pagani uocant
last_rejected.why: Missing "unde" (whence/where from): the question is origin/source of divinations, not just "where divinations come from" in a loose sense. The Latin asks from whom/what source they derive.
last_rejected.fix: whence divinations come—whether from demons or from whatever beings they are whom the pagans call gods
last_rejected.ruling: 'Where...come from' correctly renders 'unde sint'; source/origin is captured adequately.
